soil-env-279.title: Methane, the gas behind a third of near-term heating
soil-env-279.text: Rising methane emissions cause up to one-third of the global heating expected in the near term. Methane emissions are the release of this potent greenhouse gas to the air, from human activities and from natural sources such as wetlands. In 2019 about 60% came from people and 40% from nature. Most natural methane is made by methanogens, microbes that produce it in warm, moist soils and in animal guts, the process described in {{ref:soil-chem-129}}. Wetlands supply about three-quarters of the enduring natural sources. Farming copies them. Plant agriculture contributes about 15% of human emissions, and rice is the largest single source. Waterlogged paddies behave like wetlands: in 2022 they emitted about 30 million of 400 million tonnes. Land use shifts the balance too. Converting forests to farmland adds nitrogen to the soil, and that nitrogen inhibits methane oxidation, the microbial breakdown of methane. Moving the water table up or down can switch a soil between methane source and methane sink, a theme taken up in {{ref:soil-env-283}}.

soil-env-280.title: Methanotrophs, the microbes that eat methane
soil-env-280.text: Some microbes make their living from the very gas that methanogens release. Methanotrophs are bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of both carbon and energy. They live in wetlands, soils, marshes, rice paddies and landfills, mostly close to methane sources, though some oxidize methane straight from the atmosphere. By cutting the methane that reaches the air, they play a significant part in the global methane budget. Aerobic methanotrophs combine oxygen with methane. Enzymes called methane monooxygenases perform the first step. The products are formaldehyde, which is built into organic compounds, and carbon dioxide. Two groups divide the territory. Type I methanotrophs tend to dominate cold, oxygen-poor, methane-rich settings. Type II are more stress-tolerant and dominate methane-limited and acidic ones. In anoxic soils, rice paddies and sediments, some methanotrophs oxidize methane with nitrate, nitrite, iron, sulfate or manganese instead of oxygen.

soil-env-278.title: Counting the carbon that land use adds and removes
soil-env-278.text: Clearing a forest for farmland releases carbon that no smokestack ever emitted. Greenhouse gas inventories record it in a sector called land use, land-use change and forestry, or LULUCF. It covers the emissions and removals that result from how people use land, change its use and manage forests. These activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or take it out, through their effects on the carbon cycle, but they are hard to measure. The IPCC estimates that land-use change, such as turning forest into farmland, adds a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt of carbon a year. Fossil fuels and cement add 6.3 ± 0.6 Gt. Updated assessments put LULUCF emissions at 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt of carbon, or 4.1 ± 2.6 Gt of carbon dioxide, a year over 2014–2023. Under the Kyoto rules the activities fall into two classes. Accounting is mandatory for afforestation, reforestation and {{ref:soil-env-269}}. It is voluntary for managing forests, cropland and grazing land. Carbon is not the whole story. Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration, and a 2021 study found it had affected 17% of land between 1960 and 2019.

soil-env-272.title: How long biochar keeps its carbon locked away
soil-env-272.text: Biochar counts as carbon removal only if the carbon stays put. Its permanence is how long that carbon remains stored before returning to the atmosphere. Multi-pool models give biochar in soil a turnover of centuries to millennia, depending on feedstock, production conditions, application rate and site. Biochar made above 600 °C resembles inertinite, a stable component of coal. Under certain conditions 97% of its organic carbon is highly refractory, meaning it resists decay. The question is not settled. Some studies report turnover within a century. Re-analyses argue that the common two-pool decay model behind them is badly parameterised, so permanence is generally underestimated. Part of the trouble is what gets measured. Incubation experiments have mostly tracked the labile, easily decayed fraction, which falls from about 16% to 1% across production temperatures of 350–800 °C.

soil-env-273.title: Selling biochar's stored carbon as credits
soil-env-273.text: In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases. Biochar carbon credits are certified credits for carbon dioxide removed by making biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets. Abatement costs are high, so these credits sell at prices an order of magnitude above credits from emission reductions. Standards such as the European Biochar Certificate list the permissible feedstocks. Certified suppliers must also be carbon net-negative, removing more carbon than they emit.

soil-env-271.title: Letting rice paddies dry out to cut methane
soil-env-271.text: Rice need not stand in water all season. Alternate wetting and drying, or AWD, lets lowland rice fields dry for a few days before they are flooded again. In 'safe' AWD a perforated tube shows the water table. When it falls 15 cm below the soil surface, the field is re-flooded to 5 cm, and it stays flooded at flowering. Each dry spell ends the anaerobic conditions in which methane forms. Seasonal methane emissions fell by up to 85%, and the 2006 IPCC methodology assumes an average cut of 48%. AWD also saves about 38% of water without harming yields, and drying lowers arsenic and cadmium in the grain. The main drawback is higher nitrous oxide emissions. It suits areas where soils can be drained in 5-day intervals, mainly in the dry season.

soil-env-274.title: Three escape routes for wetland methane
soil-env-274.text: Methane made in a wetland soil still has to get out, and it has three routes. The water table marks the boundary. Below it, in soil without oxygen, methane is produced; above it, in aerated soil, methanotrophs consume it. A low water table forces rising methane past these microbes. The first route is molecular diffusion. It is slow through peat full of undecayed organic matter and matters more in drier, loosely packed soils, since methane moves faster through soil than through water. The second runs through aerenchyma, porous tissue in some plants. It shunts methane straight from the roots to the air, bypassing oxidation. The third is ebullition, or bubbling. Methane builds up in soil pockets until the pressure bursts them, releasing it too fast for methanotrophs to consume. Piezometers detect these pockets.

soil-env-275.title: What decides how much wetland methane escapes
soil-env-275.text: A wetland's methane output is a race between makers and eaters. Net flux depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it. Four controls set the result: water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production. Large fluxes have followed drought-driven drops in the water table. With water at or above the surface, bubbling and transport through plants dominate. Soil temperature sets how fast microbes produce and consume methane, and with the water table it drives seasonal cycles. Substrate matters too. Soils rich in acetate, or in hydrogen and carbon dioxide, favor production, and a steady supply of cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 are optimal.

soil-env-277.title: Draining a wetland can cut methane, or raise it
soil-env-277.text: Wetlands are drained for development, housing and farming, and the effect on methane is mixed. Lowering the water table increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs. That can turn a wetland from a methane source into a sink. The drains themselves can undo the gain. Ditches that stay saturated, especially when drains sit too close together, become warm, wet mini-wetlands that emit much methane.

soil-env-276.title: Wetland nitrous oxide, flowing both ways
soil-env-276.text: Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential 300 times that of carbon dioxide. It is also the leading ozone-depleting emission of the 21st century. Wetland soils exchange it with the air in either direction. Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, raise the outward flux through denitrification and nitrification. In mangroves of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, measured fluxes ranged from 0.14 to 23.83 micromoles of nitrous oxide per square meter per hour. Negative fluxes are common as well: the soil consumes the gas instead of releasing it.

soil-env-284.title: Computer models that put soil into the climate
soil-env-284.text: Climate forecasts need a ground floor. Land surface models represent vegetation, soil and terrain inside simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles. Such a model combines vegetation cover, soil type and terrain with rainfall data. It then estimates how much water soaks into the ground and how much becomes streamflow. Earth system models go further, extending climate models to include the biosphere and land use change. Even under identical emission scenarios, they predict a wide range of future carbon uptake by land and ocean. One gap stands out. The main Earth system models still omit peatlands, although peatland carbon balance is expected to shift from sink to source this century.

soil-env-283.title: Soils that swallow methane
soil-env-283.text: Soil can soak up methane as well as release it. Methanotrophic microbes in soils consume methane, including methane from the atmosphere, which makes soils a natural methane sink. Land use can weaken that sink. Converting forests and natural land to farmland raises soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation by methanotrophs. Water decides the balance most directly. Changing the water table shifts a soil between methane source and sink, and lowering a wetland's water table can make it a sink. Even landfills can help: nutrient-supplemented cover soils, rich in methanotrophs, can act as small methane sinks.

soil-env-281.title: Rewetting drained peatlands by blocking the drains
soil-env-281.text: A drained peatland heals by getting wet again. Peatland rewetting returns the land to its original waterlogged state, so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate once more. Workers keep the soil moist and slow drainage by blocking and filling canals and digging deep wells. Peat itself makes good dams. Unoxidized peat dug from the channel bottom is stable, impermeable and resistant to erosion. Plastic dams of interlocking piling can hold deep pools, but they work only on peat, not on mineral soil.

soil-env-282.title: Paludiculture: farming a peatland that stays wet
soil-env-282.text: Rewetting a peatland need not end farming on it. Paludiculture rewets drained peatlands and keeps farming them with crops suited to wet conditions, such as berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel. Raising the water table restores a peatland ecosystem that stores large amounts of carbon. The same land then serves as both carbon sink and farmland. It can also fix an old problem. Degraded farmed peatlands are often nutrient-rich, and paludiculture can remove the excess nutrients over time, a cheaper alternative to stripping the topsoil.

soil-env-269.title: Deforestation and the soil left behind
soil-env-269.text: Forests now cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread. Half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees and the conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 nearly 90% of global deforestation came from cropland expansion and the creation of pasture. The soil feels the change quickly. Topsoil often erodes once the trees are gone, and rivers carry more sediment. Tree roots bind soil, so cleared slopes become more prone to landslides. Clearing also alters soil microbial communities and reduces soil properties such as hydraulic conductivity, and sandier soils suffer more than clayey ones. In a simulation of the Amazon, surface and soil temperatures rose by 1 to 3 °C after clearing. The changed soil properties could even turn the soil into a carbon source. Repeated slash-and-burn with shortened fallows, the rest periods between crops, leaves less vegetation and lower soil biomass on burned land.

soil-env-313.title: Rangeland management, a lesson of the Dust Bowl
soil-env-313.text: The Dust Bowl showed what overgrazing and misuse of arid land could do, and rangeland management grew up in the United States in response. It is the science and practice of conserving rangelands and managing them sustainably, adjusting their parts to yield the best mix of goods and services over time. At first it focused on grazing and the proper use of range vegetation by livestock. Today it aims to protect and enhance soils, riparian zones, watersheds and vegetation while still producing meat, water, wood and fiber. Its scope has widened to the benefits described in {{ref:soil-env-285}}. Growing degradation, such as woody plant encroachment, makes rehabilitation part of the job. Climate adds pressure: heatwaves, droughts and floods are expected to alter rangelands' ecological states and cut forage production. The field draws on animal science, plant ecology, soil science, wildlife management, climatology and anthropology.

soil-env-270.title: When farmers give up the land
soil-env-270.text: Land farmed hard for a long time is sometimes simply given up. Land abandonment is that giving up of farmed land. In areas with a long history of intensive farming, threshold effects of land degradation may lead to it. Trees and shrubs then often re-establish on the former fields, a process called woody plant encroachment. Climate change may add to the pressure. Farmland values in parts of southern Europe are projected to fall by more than 80% by 2100, which could cause abandonment.

soil-env-308.title: Rain gardens, where city runoff sinks in and gets cleaned
soil-env-308.text: Every roof and road sends rain racing toward the drains, carrying pollutants with it. A rain garden, also called a bioretention facility, is a designed planted site that lets this runoff soak into the soil and be cleaned. Plants and natural or engineered soil hold the stormwater, delay its infiltration, and filter and remediate its pollutants. Deep roots open extra channels for water and keep the soil permeable. They also sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen. The cleaning works by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition. A typical garden removes about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals. A 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%. Rain gardens restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes. Unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers, though, they may not reduce pollution.

soil-env-306.title: Urban soil: stripped, packed down and polluted
soil-env-306.text: City soil carries the marks of construction and industry. Urban soil is soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity. Compared with similar soil in the wild, it holds more heavy metals, especially lead, copper and nickel, and has a lower pH. Without its topsoil it has low aeration, porosity and drainage. Compaction and contamination limit root growth and tree health. Contamination persists in cities with a history of industry, leaded gasoline or lead-based house paint. The Polish soil classification's 'urban soils' type corresponds to Urbic, Mollic or Ecranic Technosols in the WRB. Managing urban soil draws on many disciplines. It aims to protect soil biodiversity, cut industrial pollution and make soils more resilient to construction compaction. The damage can be reversed. In a Palermo trial, de-sealing long-sealed soils and replanting them stabilized infiltration and raised microbial activity within eighteen months.

soil-env-311.title: Spoil tips and the disaster at Aberfan
soil-env-311.text: In October 1966 a spoil tip at Aberfan, Wales, collapsed onto a school and killed 144 people. It had been built over a spring and was saturated by heavy rain. A spoil tip is a pile of spoil, the waste earth removed during mining or large excavations. Spoil may be ordinary soil and rock or heavily contaminated with chemical waste. Clean spoil can be used for land reclamation. Tips trap solar heat, which hinders plants and encourages erosion and unstable slopes. They also cause acid rock drainage and leach noxious chemicals into groundwater. Regreening uses geotextiles to control erosion while the site is resoiled and seeded. Old tips may later shelter rare plants, but without nearby seed sources invasive species dominate.

soil-env-312.title: Growing trees in cramped city soil
soil-env-312.text: A street tree lives in a hard place. Urban forestry is the care and management of single trees and tree populations in towns and cities to improve the urban environment. Street trees face limited soil volume, high compaction and harsh microclimates, so they grow and survive less well than trees elsewhere. Species are chosen to tolerate alkaline and compacted soils, low soil volume, de-icing salts and drought. A healthy large tree needs about 1,000 cubic feet of soil. In return, canopies intercept rain, and roots slow and filter water and return it to the air. Urban forests also support nutrient cycling and soil formation.

soil-env-309.title: The engineered soil inside a rain garden
soil-env-309.text: The soil in a rain garden is a recipe. A bioretention soil mix is the engineered growing soil through which the garden filters its water. A typical mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil. More compost improves filtering; more sand speeds infiltration but may retain fewer nutrients. The sandy mix must not be blended with less sandy surrounding soil. Clay would settle between the sand grains into a concrete-like mass that drains poorly. Where native soil drains too slowly, as Type D soils do, it should be replaced and an underdrain installed. Yet a five-year USGS study found rain gardens in urban clay soils worked without either, if infiltration before installation was at least 0.25 inches per hour.

soil-env-307.title: Artefacts, the human objects buried in soil
soil-env-307.text: Fragments of pottery, tile and animal bone turn up in dark earth. Such objects are artefacts in soil: things recognizably made or extracted from the earth by humans. They are a defining feature of human-made soils. A significant amount of artefacts, a geotechnical liner or a seal of technic hard material qualifies a soil as a Technosol. The WRB also marks human-transported natural material, with the horizon suffix τ.

soil-env-310.title: Saving dug-up topsoil in a stockpile
soil-env-310.text: Topsoil dug out for a building need not be lost. A soil stockpile is a pile of topsoil excavated during construction of buildings or infrastructure and kept for later use. Once the construction infrastructure is removed, the soil goes into landscaping or restoration. That makes it a resource for both construction and ecology. Before it is reused, the stockpiled soil may be tested for contamination.

soil-env-285.title: Ecosystem services, the work nature does for people
soil-env-285.text: New York City faced a $6–8 billion bill for a water filtration plant. Instead it restored its Catskill watershed for $1–1.5 billion. There, soil absorption and filtration, roots and soil microbes brought the water back to standard. That work is an ecosystem service, one of the many benefits people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control. The UN Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularized four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services. Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, make the others possible, from food supply to flood regulation and water purification. Regulating services include decomposing and detoxifying wastes. Erosion regulation affects people indirectly, through environmental conditions. Evaluations of ecosystem services may assign them an economic value.

soil-agri-169.title: Treating household sewage in the backyard soil
soil-agri-169.text: Where no public sewer reaches, a house must handle its own wastewater. An onsite sewage facility treats and disposes of effluent on the property that produces it. Most are conventional systems: a septic tank plus a subsurface infiltration system. Such systems handle about 25% of domestic wastewater in the US. Decomposition by natural organisms remains the main disposal mechanism. Rules therefore set minimum retention times and distances to surface water and wells. Site evaluation characterizes soils, slopes and local hydrology and geology to set the design and placement of each component. Poor siting, design or maintenance makes systems fail. Septic systems are the third most common source of pollution in US groundwater.

openers.urban-and-human-made-soils: Cities remake their soil as thoroughly as their streets. In towns, soil is often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity. Mining and large excavations leave piles of waste earth, while building sites dig out topsoil and keep it for later use. Some soils are even defined by the objects people made and left in them. This chapter follows that human-made ground and the ways people work with it, from designed planted sites that let runoff from roofs and roads soak in and be cleaned to the care of city trees.

reviews.urban-and-human-made-soils: Every soil in this chapter carries a human signature. Urban soil, stripped of topsoil, compacted and laden with lead, copper and nickel, limits roots and tree health, so urban forestry picks species that tolerate compacted soil and low soil volume. Rain gardens turn the same city surfaces to use, sending runoff through an engineered bioretention soil mix that filters out suspended solids, heavy metals and nutrients. Construction and mining move soil in bulk: stockpiles save topsoil for later restoration, while spoil tips can trap heat, erode, leach chemicals and, at Aberfan, collapse with deadly force. Artefacts record that history in the soil itself, and enough of them make a soil a Technosol.
